A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoJudge and contain readable main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be reliably matched across renumbering, relocation, and the later version's extensions.

before.justification: v2 reports original GSM8K and LiveCodeBench evaluations, inference benchmarks, and appendix experiments on classifiers, numerical precision, and task transfer.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical evaluations and adds experiments involving EAGLE-2, additional tasks, manual annotation, heuristic comparisons, and energy consumption.

M1.justification: The core mining, classifier-training, and verification pipeline remains unchanged. Appendix L introduces a localized mining adaptation: judge each alternative against the current running response and accept it when no worse, replacing equivalence against the initial target answer. Appendix J also implements integration with EAGLE-2 drafting heads.

E1.justification: Beyond retained GSM8K and LiveCodeBench coverage, v4 evaluates closed-book TriviaQA, Arena-Hard-Auto-v2.0 creative writing, MATH-hard, and synthetic GSM8K prompts containing 8–10K context tokens. Appendix N additionally uses ARC-Challenge and Alpaca examples to train the manually annotated classifier.

E2.justification: v4 adds EAGLE-2 versus EAGLE-2 with AutoJudge (Figure 12), mathematical-token heuristics and combinations with Top-K (Table 10), and a manually annotated classifier (Appendix N). The manual experiment reconstructs aspects of Judge Decoding; the original implementation and annotated dataset remain unavailable according to both PDFs.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 replaces shared 32-token windows with independently tuned windows. Tuning already appeared in v2 Appendix G, but v4 also expands its search grid to include six tokens. Added settings include Qwen2.5-32B, eight-token EAGLE windows, and new task-specific splits and judge-based metrics. Appendix M.2 inconsistently describes whether the long-context classifier was trained on short or long contexts.

E4.justification: v4 adds tests of mathematical rules versus learned importance, manual versus automatic annotation, transfer to harder mathematics, behavior under long contexts, and the relationship between draft confidence and classifier predictions. It also adds energy measurements and investigates creative-writing failures. Earlier classifier, precision, and GSM8K–LiveCodeBench transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix L newly specifies three Claude Sonnet 4 judgments per comparison, aggregated through majority and tie rules to address inconsistent judgments. This is a repeated-evaluation procedure for the new experiments, not evidence of increased runs for retained benchmarks. Main timing and accuracy results still lack confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerous timing entries change, alongside substantial new results. In the retained 32-token-window 8B/70B comparison, AutoJudge at threshold 0.031 changes from 94.6 to 80.6 tokens/s, while the baseline changes from 49.2 to 40.6 (v2 Table 1; v4 Table 4). New results cover additional models, tasks, comparators, and energy consumption. Most original accuracy and classifier-ablation plots are retained.

T1.justification: The mismatch definitions, search formulation, and Gumbel-max sampling construction in Section 3.1 and Appendix A remain substantively unchanged. The new judge adaptation is described procedurally; no new formal theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central annotation-free acceleration claims and headline speed–accuracy claims. The conclusion now explicitly claims demonstrated speedups over tuned speculative decoding and EAGLE, whereas v2 left advanced-decoding integration to future work, and extends its empirical claim beyond mathematics and programming.

C2.justification: v2 presents open-ended use as untested; v4 identifies creative writing as a failure case and attributes its limited acceleration to subjective, noisy judgments, with over 70% of mismatches labeled important. New discussions interpret harder-task transfer, manual-annotation weaknesses, mathematical rules missing planning steps, and the weak relationship between draft confidence and learned importance.

D1.justification: v4 adds concrete reproduction information for the extensions: EAGLE head access and depth/window settings, the exact Claude judge version and voting rules, new dataset construction procedures, manual annotation effort of 8–10 hours, and energy measurement using nvidia-smi and inference time. Existing core software versions, hardware descriptions, and code access are largely retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting ARC, TriviaQA, Arena-Hard, Alpaca, and energy measurement, and removes the MMLU-Pro reference. Positioning as an automated extension of Judge Decoding remains, supplemented by the reconstructed manual comparison. EAGLE-2 was already cited in v2.

P1.justification: v4 edits grammar, terminology, affiliation and publication-header text, and rewrites the experimental overview, runtime discussion, limitations, and conclusion. The overall introduction–background–method–experiments structure remains. Most additional appendix prose documents new experiments rather than extensively rewriting existing explanations.

P2.justification: v4 splits the original three-panel Figure 3 into separate Llama and expanded Qwen displays, reorganizes timing tables, and brings offloading results into the main text. It adds EAGLE, open-ended-task, transfer, and manual-annotation figures plus heuristic and energy tables, while resizing or relocating several retained plots.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical support and applicability boundaries: independently tuned timing comparisons become primary, EAGLE integration is tested, and new comparator and generalization studies examine previously untested scope, including failures. These changes make the acceleration and generality claims more assessable. The approximate manual comparison and inconsistencies in long-context training and offloading accuracy descriptions weaken particular conclusions, but do not outweigh the broader gains in validation and qualification.
